claim: Four intergenerational adaptations to stress in C. elegans (bacterial infection, eukaryotic infection, osmotic stress, and nutrient stress) are conserved in at least one other Caenorhabditis species.
source: We found that all four intergenerational physiological adaptations are conserved in at least one other species
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding based on experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Intergenerational adaptations to stress are stress-specific.
source: We found that all four intergenerational physiological adaptations are conserved in at least one other species, that they are stress -specific
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, supported by experimental data showing distinct responses to different stresses.

claim: Intergenerational adaptations to stress have deleterious tradeoffs in mismatched environments.
source: We found that all four intergenerational physiological adaptations are conserved in at least one other species, that they are stress -specific, and that they have deleterious tradeoffs in mismatched environments.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, supported by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: 587 genes exhibited a greater than twofold intergenerational change in expression in response to stress in C. elegans and at least one other species.
source: By profiling the effects of parental bacterial infection and osmotic stress exposure on progeny gene expression across species, we established a core set of 587 genes that exhibited a greater than twofold intergenerational change in expression in response to stress in C. elegans and at least one other species
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding based on RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: 37 genes exhibited a greater than twofold intergenerational change in expression in all four species tested in response to stress.
source: as well as a set of 37 highly conserved genes that exhibited a greater than twofold intergenerational change in expression in all four species tested.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding based on RNA-seq data analysis across species.

claim: Presumed adaptive and deleterious intergenerational effects are molecularly related at the gene expression level.
source: Furthermore, we provide evidence suggesting that presumed adaptive and deleterious intergenerational effects are molecularly related at the gene expression level.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, supported by data showing inversions in gene expression patterns correlating with phenotypic inversions.

claim: None of the effects of parental stress on C. elegans F1 progeny gene expression persisted transgenerationally three generations after stress exposure.
source: Lastly, we found that none of the effects we detected of these stresses on C. elegans F1 progeny gene expression persisted transgenerationally three generations after stress exposure.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding based on F3 RNA-seq data.

claim: The vast majority of the effects of parental stress on progeny gene expression are reversible and not maintained transgenerationally.
source: We conclude that intergenerational responses to stress play a substantial and evolutionarily conserved role in regulating animal physiology and that the vast majority of the effects of parental stress on progeny gene expression are reversible and not maintained transgenerationally.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this conclusion based on F1 and F3 gene expression data.

claim: C. elegans, C. briggsae, C. kamaaina, and C. tropicalis shared a last common ancestor approximately 30 million years ago.
source: We tested if these four intergenerational adaptive responses were conserved in four different species of Caenorhabditis (C. briggsae, C. elegans, C. kamaaina, and C. tropicalis) that shared a last common ancestor approximately 30 million years ago and have diverged to the point of having approximately 0.05 substitutions per site at the nucleotide level (Figure 1A; Cutter, 2008).
evidence: The text cites Cutter, 2008 as the source for this evolutionary timing.

claim: The four Caenorhabditis species studied have diverged to the point of having approximately 0.05 substitutions per site at the nucleotide level.
source: We tested if these four intergenerational adaptive responses were conserved in four different species of Caenorhabditis (C. briggsae, C. elegans, C. kamaaina, and C. tropicalis) that shared a last common ancestor approximately 30 million years ago and have diverged to the point of having approximately 0.05 substitutions per site at the nucleotide level (Figure 1A; Cutter, 2008).
evidence: The text cites Cutter, 2008 as the source for this divergence measure.

claim: Parental exposure to P. vranovensis protects offspring from future infection in C. elegans.
source: We found that parental exposure to the bacterial pathogen P. vranovensis protected offspring from future infection in both C. elegans and C. kamaaina (Figure 1B)
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 1B showing the experimental data.

claim: Parental exposure to P. vranovensis protects offspring from future infection in C. kamaaina.
source: We found that parental exposure to the bacterial pathogen P. vranovensis protected offspring from future infection in both C. elegans and C. kamaaina (Figure 1B)
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 1B showing the experimental data.

claim: The intergenerational adaptive effect to P. vranovensis in C. kamaaina requires cysl-1 and rhy-1.
source: and that this adaptive intergenerational effect in C. kamaaina required the same stress response genes (cysl-1 and rhy-1) as previously reported for C. elegans (Burton et al., 2020; Figure 1C)
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding, references Burton et al., 2020, and cites Figure 1C showing the experimental data.

claim: Naive C. briggsae animals are more resistant to P. vranovensis than C. elegans, C. kamaaina, and C. tropicalis.
source: By contrast, we found that naive C. briggsae animals were more resistant to P. vranovensis than any of the other species tested
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding, which is supported by data in Figure 1B.

claim: Parental exposure of C. briggsae to P. vranovensis causes greater than 99% of offspring to die upon future exposure to P. vranovensis.
source: but exposure of C. briggsae parents to P. vranovensis caused greater than 99% of offspring to die upon future exposure to P. vranovensis (Figure 1B).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 1B showing the experimental data.

claim: Parental exposure to P. vranovensis has no observable effect on offspring response to infection in C. tropicalis.
source: Parental exposure to P. vranovensis had no observable effect on offspring response to infection in C. tropicalis (Figure 1B).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 1B showing the experimental data.

claim: Parental exposure to mild osmotic stress protects offspring from future osmotic stress in C. elegans.
source: we found that parental exposure to mild osmotic stress protected offspring from future osmotic stress in C. elegans, C. briggsae, and C. kamaaina, but again not in C. tropicalis (Figure 1D).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 1D showing the experimental data.

claim: Parental exposure to mild osmotic stress protects offspring from future osmotic stress in C. briggsae.
source: we found that parental exposure to mild osmotic stress protected offspring from future osmotic stress in C. elegans, C. briggsae, and C. kamaaina, but again not in C. tropicalis (Figure 1D).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 1D showing the experimental data.

claim: Parental exposure to mild osmotic stress protects offspring from future osmotic stress in C. kamaaina.
source: we found that parental exposure to mild osmotic stress protected offspring from future osmotic stress in C. elegans, C. briggsae, and C. kamaaina, but again not in C. tropicalis (Figure 1D).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 1D showing the experimental data.

claim: Parental exposure to mild osmotic stress does not protect offspring from future osmotic stress in C. tropicalis.
source: we found that parental exposure to mild osmotic stress protected offspring from future osmotic stress in C. elegans, C. briggsae, and C. kamaaina, but again not in C. tropicalis (Figure 1D).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 1D showing the experimental data.

claim: The intergenerational adaptation to osmotic stress in C. briggsae requires gpdh-2.
source: This intergenerational adaptation to osmotic stress in C. briggsae and C. kamaaina required the glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase gpdh-2 (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 1E showing the experimental data.

claim: The intergenerational adaptation to osmotic stress in C. kamaaina requires gpdh-2.
source: This intergenerational adaptation to osmotic stress in C. briggsae and C. kamaaina required the glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase gpdh-2 (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 1—figure supplement 1D showing the experimental data.

claim: N. parisii can infect C. kamaaina.
source: Here, we show that N. parisii can also infect C. kamaaina and C. tropicalis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E-G).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 1—figure supplement 1E-G showing the experimental data.

claim: N. parisii can infect C. tropicalis.
source: Here, we show that N. parisii can also infect C. kamaaina and C. tropicalis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E-G).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 1—figure supplement 1E-G showing the experimental data.

claim: Parental exposure of C. elegans to N. parisii protects offspring from future infection.
source: By investigating the effects of parental N. parisii infection on offspring across species, we found that parental exposure of C. elegans and C. briggsae to N. parisii protected offspring from future infection (Figure 1F).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 1F showing the experimental data.

claim: Parental exposure of C. briggsae to N. parisii protects offspring from future infection.
source: By investigating the effects of parental N. parisii infection on offspring across species, we found that parental exposure of C. elegans and C. briggsae to N. parisii protected offspring from future infection (Figure 1F).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 1F showing the experimental data.

claim: Parental exposure of C. kamaaina to N. parisii has no observable effect on offspring infection rate.
source: By contrast, parental exposure of C. kamaaina and C. tropicalis to N. parisii had no observable effect on offspring infection rate (Figure 1F).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 1F showing the experimental data.

claim: Parental exposure of C. tropicalis to N. parisii has no observable effect on offspring infection rate.
source: By contrast, parental exposure of C. kamaaina and C. tropicalis to N. parisii had no observable effect on offspring infection rate (Figure 1F).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 1F showing the experimental data.

claim: Parental nutrient stress by food deprivation results in larger offspring in C. elegans.
source: We found that parental nutrient stress by food deprivation resulted in larger offspring in both C. elegans and C. tropicalis, which is predicted to be adaptive (Hibshman et al., 2016), but had minimal effects on offspring size in C. briggsae and C. kamaaina (Figure 1G).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding, references Hibshman et al., 2016, and cites Figure 1G showing the experimental data.

claim: Parental nutrient stress by food deprivation results in larger offspring in C. tropicalis.
source: We found that parental nutrient stress by food deprivation resulted in larger offspring in both C. elegans and C. tropicalis, which is predicted to be adaptive (Hibshman et al., 2016), but had minimal effects on offspring size in C. briggsae and C. kamaaina (Figure 1G).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding, references Hibshman et al., 2016, and cites Figure 1G showing the experimental data.

claim: Parental nutrient stress by food deprivation has minimal effects on offspring size in C. briggsae.
source: We found that parental nutrient stress by food deprivation resulted in larger offspring in both C. elegans and C. tropicalis, which is predicted to be adaptive (Hibshman et al., 2016), but had minimal effects on offspring size in C. briggsae and C. kamaaina (Figure 1G).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 1G showing the experimental data.

claim: Parental nutrient stress by food deprivation has minimal effects on offspring size in C. kamaaina.
source: We found that parental nutrient stress by food deprivation resulted in larger offspring in both C. elegans and C. tropicalis, which is predicted to be adaptive (Hibshman et al., 2016), but had minimal effects on offspring size in C. briggsae and C. kamaaina (Figure 1G).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 1G showing the experimental data.

claim: Parental exposure to P. vranovensis results in substantial changes in offspring gene expression in all four Caenorhabditis species investigated.
source: Consistent with previous observations in C. elegans, we found that parental exposure to P. vranovensis resulted in substantial changes in offspring gene expression in all four species we investigated (Figure 2 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 2 and Supplementary file 2 showing the RNA-seq data.

claim: 367 genes exhibited a greater than twofold change in expression in the offspring of P. vranovensis-infected animals in C. elegans and at least one other species.
source: Of the 7587 single-copy orthologs shared between the four species, we identified 367 genes that exhibited a greater than twofold change in expression in the offspring of infected animals in C. elegans (padj <0.01) and at least one other species (Figure 2D and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 2D and Supplementary file 2 showing the RNA-seq data.

claim: 35 genes exhibited a greater than twofold change in expression in the offspring of parents exposed to P. vranovensis in all four species.
source: Furthermore, we found that 35 genes exhibited a greater than twofold change in expression (padj <0.01) in the offspring of parents exposed to P. vranovensis in all four species (Figure 2D and Table 1).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 2D and Table 1 showing the RNA-seq data.

claim: Parental exposure to osmotic stress resulted in 235 genes exhibiting differential expression in both C. elegans and C. briggsae offspring.
source: From this analysis, we observed that parental exposure to osmotic stress resulted in 235 genes exhibiting differential expression in both C. elegans and C. briggsae offspring (Figure 2F–J and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 2F–J and Supplementary file 3 showing the RNA-seq data.

claim: Gene expression changes in offspring from parents exposed to osmotic stress are largely distinct from those observed in offspring from parents exposed to P. vranovensis.
source: In addition, we found that these changes in gene expression were largely distinct from the gene expression changes observed in the offspring of parents exposed to P. vranovensis (Figure 2K and Supplementary files 2 and 3)
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 2K and Supplementary files 2 and 3 showing the RNA-seq data.

claim: Parental exposure of C. kamaaina to osmotic stress resulted in approximately fivefold fewer changes in offspring gene expression compared to C. elegans.
source: However, parental exposure to C. kamaaina and C. tropicalis to osmotic stress resulted in approximately fivefold fewer changes in offspring gene expression (Figure 2G–H and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 2G–H and Supplementary file 3 showing the RNA-seq data.

claim: Parental exposure of C. tropicalis to osmotic stress resulted in approximately fivefold fewer changes in offspring gene expression compared to C. elegans.
source: However, parental exposure to C. kamaaina and C. tropicalis to osmotic stress resulted in approximately fivefold fewer changes in offspring gene expression (Figure 2G–H and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 2G–H and Supplementary file 3 showing the RNA-seq data.

claim: Five genes (C30B5.6, hphd-1, C42D4.3, ttr-15, and F08F3.4) exhibited differential expression in the offspring of parents exposed to osmotic stress in all four species.
source: In total five genes (C30B5.6, hphd-1, C42D4.3, ttr-15, and F08F3.4) exhibited differential expression in the offspring of parents exposed to osmotic stress in all four species (Figure 2I and Table 1)
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 2I and Table 1 showing the RNA-seq data.

claim: Three genes (C30B5.6, hphd-1, and C42D4.3) changed in the offspring of parents exposed to both P. vranovensis and osmotic stress in all four species.
source: and three of these five (C30B5.6, hphd-1, and C42D4.3) were also observed to change in the offspring of parents exposed to P. vranovensis (Table 1).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Table 1 showing the RNA-seq data.

claim: The 37 genes that exhibit changes in expression in the offspring of stressed parents in all four species are significantly enriched for extracellular proteins.
source: We found that these 37 genes were significantly enriched for extracellular proteins (p < 2.278 × 10–3).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding based on gene ontology analysis using g:Profiler.

claim: Of the 562 genes that exhibited a greater than twofold change in expression in the offspring of parents exposed to P. vranovensis in C. elegans, only 54 also exhibited a greater than twofold intergenerational change in expression in C. kamaaina.
source: We found that of the 562 genes that exhibited a greater than twofold change in expression in the offspring of parents exposed to P. vranovensis in C. elegans, only 54 also exhibited a greater than twofold intergenerational change in expression in C. kamaaina (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding based on RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: 17 genes exhibited consistent changes in C. elegans and C. kamaaina but either did not change or changed in the opposite direction in C. briggsae in response to parental P. vranovensis exposure.
source: From this refined list of 54 genes, 17 genes either did not exhibit a change in C. briggsae or changed in the opposite direction (Table 2).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Table 2 showing the RNA-seq data.

claim: All three genes previously reported to be required for the intergenerational adaptation to P. vranovensis (rhy-1, cysl-1, and cysl-2) were among the 17 genes that exhibited differential expression in C. elegans and C. kamaaina but not in C. briggsae.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis that intergenerational gene expression changes across species might correlate with their phenotypic responses, we found that all three genes previously reported to be required for the intergenerational adaptation to P. vranovensis (rhy-1, cysl-1, and cysl-2 – Burton et al., 2020) were among the 17 genes that exhibited differential expression in C. elegans and C. kamaaina but not in C. briggsae.
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding, referencing Burton et al., 2020 and RNA-seq data.

claim: The overlap of genes required for intergenerational adaptation to P. vranovensis with genes showing species-specific expression patterns is significantly above what is expected by chance (P < 1.337e−08).
source: This overlap is significantly above what is expected by chance (P < 1.337e−−08 – hypergeometric probability).
evidence: The text explicitly states this statistical finding based on hypergeometric probability analysis.

claim: rhy-1 exhibited a greater than twofold increase in expression in C. elegans and C. kamaaina F1 progeny but had an inverted greater than twofold decrease in expression in C. briggsae F1 progeny in response to parental P. vranovensis exposure.
source: Notably, of the revised list of 17 genes, we identified a single gene that exhibited a greater than twofold increase in expression in C. elegans and C. kamaaina F1 progeny but had an inverted greater than twofold decrease in expression in C. briggsae F1 progeny. That gene is rhy-1 (Figure 2E)
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 2E showing the RNA-seq data.

claim: The directional change of rhy-1 expression in progeny of animals exposed to P. vranovensis correlates with whether parental exposure results in enhanced or reduced pathogen resistance in offspring.
source: This directional change of rhy-1 expression in progeny of animals exposed to P. vranovensis correlates with the observation that parental exposure to P. vranovensis results in enhanced pathogen resistance in offspring in C. elegans and C. kamaaina but has a strong deleterious effect on pathogen resistance in C. briggsae (Figure 1B).
evidence: The text explicitly states this correlation based on RNA-seq and phenotypic data.

claim: Four genes (T05F1.9, grl-21, gpdh-1, and T22B7.3) are specifically differentially expressed in the three species that adapt to osmotic stress but not in C. tropicalis.
source: From this analysis, we identified four genes (T05F1.9, grl-21, gpdh-1, and T22B7.3) that are specifically differentially expressed in the three species that adapt to osmotic stress but not in C. tropicalis (Table 2)
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Table 2 showing the RNA-seq data.

claim: gpdh-1 is one of the most upregulated genes in response to osmotic stress.
source: this list of genes includes the glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase gpdh-1 which is one of the most upregulated genes in response to osmotic stress and is known to be required for animals to properly respond to osmotic stress (Lamitina et al., 2006).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding, referencing Lamitina et al., 2006.

claim: gpdh-1 is known to be required for animals to properly respond to osmotic stress.
source: this list of genes includes the glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase gpdh-1 which is one of the most upregulated genes in response to osmotic stress and is known to be required for animals to properly respond to osmotic stress (Lamitina et al., 2006).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding, citing Lamitina et al., 2006.

claim: Approximately 50% of all genes that were differentially expressed in the offspring of stressed parents exhibit a change in gene expression that was more than one standard deviation outside their average expression across all time points of embryo development.
source: In addition, we found that approximately 50% of all genes that were differentially expressed in the offspring of stressed parents when compared to naive parents exhibited a change in gene expression that was more than one standard deviation outside their average expression across all time points of embryo development (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-C).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-C showing the analysis.

claim: None of the 1515 genes that exhibited differential expression in F1 progeny for either P. vranovensis infection or osmotic stress were also differentially expressed in C. elegans F3 progeny.
source: We found that none of the 1515 genes that exhibited differential expression in F1 progeny for either P. vranovensis infection or osmotic stress were also differentially expressed in C. elegans F3 progeny (Figure 2L and M and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 2L and M and Supplementary file 4 showing the RNA-seq data.

claim: Two genes (hphd-1 and C09B8.4 orthologs) exhibited differential expression in both the F1 and F3 progeny of C. kamaaina parents exposed to osmotic stress.
source: We did, however, identify two genes, the C. kamaaina orthologs of C. elegans hphd-1 and C09B8.4, that exhibited differential expression in both the F1 and F3 progeny of parents exposed to osmotic stress (Figure 2M and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 2M and Supplementary file 4 showing the RNA-seq data.

claim: Parental exposure to P. vranovensis does not affect the ability of C. elegans to intergenerationally adapt to osmotic stress.
source: We found that parental exposure to P. vranovensis did not affect the ability of animals to intergenerationally adapt to osmotic stress (Figure 3A).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 3A showing the experimental data.

claim: Parental exposure to osmotic stress completely eliminates the ability of C. elegans to intergenerationally adapt to P. vranovensis.
source: By contrast, parental exposure to osmotic stress completely eliminated the ability of animals to intergenerationally adapt to P. vranovensis (Figure 3B).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 3B showing the experimental data.

claim: osm-8 mutant animals that constitutively activate the osmotic stress response are completely unable to adapt to P. vranovensis infection.
source: This effect is unlikely to be due to the effects of osmotic stress on P. vranovensis itself, as mutant animals that constitutively activate the osmotic stress response (osm-8) were also completely unable to adapt to P. vranovensis infection (Figure 3C; Rohlfing et al., 2011).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding, references Rohlfing et al., 2011, and cites Figure 3C showing the experimental data.

claim: L4 parental exposure of C. elegans to N. parisii has a small, but not significant effect on offspring response to osmotic stress.
source: Here, we found that L4 parental exposure of C. elegans to N. parisii had a small, but not significant effect on offspring response to osmotic stress (Figure 3D).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 3D showing the experimental data.

claim: Parental exposure to both osmotic stress and N. parisii infection simultaneously results in offspring that are less protected against future N. parisii infection than when parents are exposed to N. parisii alone.
source: However, similar to our observations for osmotic stress and bacterial infection, we found that parental exposure to both osmotic stress and N. parisii infection simultaneously resulted in offspring that were less protected against future N. parisii infection than when parents are exposed to N. parisii alone (Figure 3E).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 3E showing the experimental data.

claim: Parental exposure to P. vranovensis has no observable effect on offspring response to N. parisii either alone or when both pathogens are present simultaneously.
source: We found that parental exposure to P. vranovnesis had no observable effect on offspring response to N. parisii either alone or when both pathogens were present simultaneously (Figure 1F).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 1F showing the experimental data.

claim: Parental exposure to N. parisii has no observable effect on offspring response to P. vranovensis either alone or when both pathogens are present at the same time.
source: Similarly, we found that parental exposure to N. parisii had no observable effect on offspring response to P. vranovensis either alone or when both pathogens were present at the same time (Figure 1G).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 1G showing the experimental data.

claim: Parental exposure to Pseudomonas sp. 15C5 enhances offspring growth rate in response to future exposure to Pseudomonas sp. 15C5.
source: From this analysis, we identified a new Pseudomonas isolate, Pseudomonas sp. 15C5, where parental exposure to Pseudomonas sp. 15C5 enhanced offspring growth rate in response to future exposure to Pseudomonas sp. 15C5 (Figure 4A).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 4A showing the experimental data.

claim: Parental exposure to either P. vranovensis or Pseudomonas sp. 15C5 protects offspring from future exposure to the other Pseudomonas isolate.
source: and we found that parental exposure to either isolate of Pseudomonas protected offspring from future exposure to the other Pseudomonas isolate (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 4A–B showing the experimental data.

claim: Pseudomonas sp. 15C5 is not an isolate of P. vranovensis and is most similar to Pseudomonas putida.
source: From this analysis, we found that Pseudomonas sp. 15C5 is not an isolate of P. vranovensis and is most similar to Pseudomonas putida – 99.49% identical 16S rRNA and 98.86% identical rpoD by BLAST (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding based on 16S rRNA and rpoD sequencing data.

claim: P. aeruginosa did not cross protect against P. vranovensis.
source: We note, however, that other pathogenic species of Pseudomonas, such as P. aeruginosa, did not cross protect against P. vranovensis (Burton et al., 2020)
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding, citing Burton et al., 2020.

claim: Parental exposure of C. elegans to Serratia plymuthica BUR1537 results in intergenerational deleterious effects.
source: In addition to these intergenerational adaptive effects, we also identified two bacterial isolates that activate pathogen–response pathways, Serretia plymutica BUR1537 and Aeromonas sp. BIGb0469 (Samuel et al., 2016; Hellberg et al., 2015), that resulted in intergenerational deleterious effects (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding, references Samuel et al., 2016 and Hellberg et al., 2015, and cites Figure 4C–D showing the experimental data.

claim: Parental exposure of C. elegans to Aeromonas sp. BIGb0469 results in intergenerational deleterious effects.
source: In addition to these intergenerational adaptive effects, we also identified two bacterial isolates that activate pathogen–response pathways, Serretia plymutica BUR1537 and Aeromonas sp. BIGb0469 (Samuel et al., 2016; Hellberg et al., 2015), that resulted in intergenerational deleterious effects (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding, references Samuel et al., 2016 and Hellberg et al., 2015, and cites Figure 4C–D showing the experimental data.

claim: Parental exposure to Serratia plymuthica BUR1537 does not intergenerationally protect animals against P. vranovensis.
source: Parental exposure of animals to these potential bacterial pathogens did not intergenerationally protect animals against P. vranovensis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 4—figure supplement 1 showing the experimental data.

claim: Parental exposure to Aeromonas sp. BIGb0469 does not intergenerationally protect animals against P. vranovensis.
source: Parental exposure of animals to these potential bacterial pathogens did not intergenerationally protect animals against P. vranovensis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 4—figure supplement 1 showing the experimental data.

claim: Only 28 genes exhibit differential expression in the offspring of parents exposed to all four potential pathogens (P. vranovensis, Pseudomonas sp. 15C5, S. plymuthica, and Aeromonas sp.).
source: We found that only 28 genes exhibit differential expression in the offspring of parents exposed to all four potential pathogens (Figure 4E–H).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 4E–H showing the RNA-seq data.

claim: 309 genes are specifically differentially expressed in the offspring of parents exposed to P. vranovensis and Pseudomonas sp. 15C5 but not in the offspring of parents exposed to S. plymuthica BUR1537 or Aeromonas sp. BIGb0469.
source: However, we identified 309 genes that are specifically differentially expressed in the offspring of parents exposed to P. vranovensis and Pseudomonas sp. 15C5 but not in the offspring of parents exposed to S. plymuthica BUR1537 or Aeromonas sp. BIGb0469 (Figure 4H and Supplementary file 7).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 4H and Supplementary file 7 showing the RNA-seq data.

claim: Intergenerational responses to stress are evolutionarily conserved.
source: Our findings demonstrate that intergenerational adaptive responses to stress are evolutionarily conserved, stress -specific, and are predominantly not maintained transgenerationally.
evidence: The text explicitly states this conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Intergenerational responses to stress are predominantly not maintained transgenerationally.
source: Our findings demonstrate that intergenerational adaptive responses to stress are evolutionarily conserved, stress -specific, and are predominantly not maintained transgenerationally.
evidence: The text explicitly states this conclusion based on F1 and F3 RNA-seq data.

claim: The mechanisms that mediate intergenerational adaptive responses in some species might be related to the mechanisms that mediate intergenerational deleterious effects in other species.
source: In addition, our findings suggest that the mechanisms that mediate intergenerational adaptive responses in some species might be related to the mechanisms that mediate intergenerational deleterious effects in other species.
evidence: The text explicitly states this suggestion based on the correlation between rhy-1 expression patterns and phenotypic outcomes.

claim: N. parisii is a common natural pathogen of both C. elegans and C. briggsae.
source: N. parisii is a common natural pathogen of both C. elegans and C. briggsae (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: The text explicitly states this fact, citing Zhang et al., 2016.

claim: Parental exposure to osmotic stress and P. vranovensis infection causes substantial changes in offspring gene expression in C. elegans.
source: Of the four intergenerational models investigated here, parental exposure of C. elegans to osmotic stress and P. vranovensis infection were previously reported to cause substantial changes in offspring gene expression, including the increased expression of genes that are required for the observed intergenerational adaptations (Burton et al., 2020; Burton et al., 2017).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding, citing Burton et al., 2020 and Burton et al., 2017.

claim: The effects of parental stress exposure on offspring gene expression resemble a subset of the transcriptional stress response observed in parental animals.
source: These effects of parental stress exposure on offspring gene expression resemble a subset of the transcriptional stress response observed in parental animals and could potentially prime offspring to respond to the same stress (Burton et al., 2020).
evidence: The text explicitly states this observation, citing Burton et al., 2020.

claim: 7587 single-copy orthologs are conserved across C. elegans, C. briggsae, C. kamaaina, and C. tropicalis.
source: This analysis allowed us to compare the effects of parental stress on offspring gene expression of 7587 single-copy orthologs that are conserved across all four species (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding based on orthology analysis.

claim: Intergenerational effects have been reported to contribute to numerous organismal phenotypes and pathologies in species ranging from plants to mammals.
source: Multigenerational effects of a parent's environment on progeny have been reported to contribute to numerous organismal phenotypes and pathologies in species ranging from plants to mammals (Agrawal et al., 1999; Bozler et al., 2019; Burton et al., 2020; Burton et al., 2017; Dantzer et al., 2013; Dias and Ressler, 2014; Hibshman et al., 2016; Houri-Zeevi et al., 2020; Jordan et al., 2019; Kaletsky et al., 2020; Kishimoto et al., 2017; Klosin et al., 2017; Luna et al., 2012; Ma et al., 2019; Moore et al., 2019; Öst et al., 2014; Palominos et al., 2017; Posner et al., 2019; Veenendaal et al., 2013; Vellichirammal et al., 2017; Webster et al., 2018; Wibowo et al., 2016; Willis et al., 2021).
evidence: The text explicitly states this claim with extensive citations to support it.

claim: Intergenerational adaptive changes can lead to substantial increases in organismal survival, with up to 50-fold increases in the survival of offspring from stressed parents being reported.
source: These intergenerational adaptive changes in development and physiology, which include effects that are sometimes interchangeably described as parental effects, can lead to substantial increases in organismal survival, with up to 50-fold increases in the survival of offspring from stressed parents being reported when compared to the offspring from naive parents (Burton et al., 2020).
evidence: The text explicitly states this claim, citing Burton et al., 2020.

claim: Some observations of intergenerational effects in mammals have been found to be physiologically adaptive.
source: Similar to findings in plants and invertebrates, some observations of intergenerational effects in mammals have been found to be physiologically adaptive (Dantzer et al., 2013)
evidence: The text explicitly states this claim, citing Dantzer et al., 2013.

claim: It has been hypothesized that under different conditions the intergenerational effects of fetal programming might be considered physiologically adaptive.
source: Nonetheless, even for these presumed deleterious intergenerational effects, it has been hypothesized that under different conditions the intergenerational effects of fetal programming, such as the effects caused by the Dutch Hunger Winter, might be considered physiologically adaptive (Hales and Barker, 2001; Hales and Barker, 1992).
evidence: The text explicitly states this hypothesis, citing Hales and Barker, 2001 and Hales and Barker, 1992.

claim: Multiple different studies have reported that some environmental stresses elicit changes in progeny physiology and gene expression that persist for three or more generations (transgenerational effects).
source: Furthermore, multiple different studies have recently reported that some environmental stresses elicit changes in progeny physiology and gene expression that persist for three or more generations, also known as transgenerational effects (Kaletsky et al., 2020; Klosin et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2019; Moore et al., 2019; Posner et al., 2019; Webster et al., 2018).
evidence: The text explicitly states this claim with citations to support it.

claim: All four models of intergenerational adaptive effects in C. elegans are conserved in at least one other species but all exhibited a different pattern of evolutionary conservation.
source: Overall, our findings support the conclusion that some types of intergenerational effects are conserved while others diverge, not unlike other important aspects of biology that vary between the species investigated here such as mode of reproduction – C. elegans, C. briggsae, and C. tropicalis are hermaphroditic while C. kamaaina is an exclusively male–female species. Specifically, our findings provide some of the first evidence that the mechanisms underlying intergenerational effects of a parent's environment on offspring are evolutionarily conserved among different species.
evidence: The text explicitly states this conclusion based on the experimental data showing different conservation patterns for different stresses.

claim: C. elegans, C. briggsae, and C. tropicalis are hermaphroditic while C. kamaaina is an exclusively male–female species.
source: not unlike other important aspects of biology that vary between the species investigated here such as mode of reproduction – C. elegans, C. briggsae, and C. tropicalis are hermaphroditic while C. kamaaina is an exclusively male–female species.
evidence: The text explicitly states this fact about the reproductive modes of these species.

claim: The 37 genes that exhibited intergenerational regulation in all species might be particularly tuned for intergenerational regulation and might be involved in intergenerational responses to stress in more distantly related species.
source: We propose that these genes might be particularly tuned for intergenerational regulation and might similarly be involved in intergenerational responses to stress in more distantly related species, including species outside the Caenorhabditis genus.
evidence: The text explicitly proposes this hypothesis based on the conservation of these genes across species.

claim: The molecular consequences of parental stress on offspring might be more easily identifiable than the specific physiological consequences.
source: We hypothesize that the molecular consequences of parental stress on offspring, such as changes in the expression of stress–response genes, might be more easily identifiable than the specific physiological consequences of parental stress on offspring.
evidence: The text explicitly states this hypothesis based on observations in C. tropicalis.

claim: Similar observations of presumed intergenerational deleterious effects in diverse species, such as fetal programming in humans, might be molecularly related to intergenerational adaptive effects in other species.
source: To our knowledge, these findings are the first to suggest that the molecular mechanisms underlying presumed adaptive and deleterious intergenerational effects in different species are evolutionarily related at the gene expression level. These findings suggest that similar observations of presumed intergenerational deleterious effects in diverse species, such as fetal programming in humans, might also be molecularly related to intergenerational adaptive effects in other species.
evidence: The text explicitly suggests this possibility based on the correlation between gene expression patterns and phenotypic outcomes.

claim: Evolutionary modeling suggests that intergenerational effects are favored when offspring environmental conditions are predictable from the parental environment.
source: Evolutionary modeling of intergenerational and transgenerational effects has suggested that different ecological pressures favor the evolution of either intergenerational or transgenerational responses under different conditions. Specifically, it has been suggested that intergenerational effects are favored when offspring environmental conditions are predictable from the parental environment (Dey et al., 2016; Lind et al., 2020; Proulx et al., 2019; Uller, 2008).
evidence: The text explicitly states this claim, citing multiple sources.

claim: It has been speculated that intergenerational adaptations to stress will have costs.
source: Furthermore, it has been speculated that intergenerational adaptations to stress will have costs (Uller, 2008).
evidence: The text explicitly states this speculation, citing Uller, 2008.

claim: Transgenerational effects are predominantly favored when parental environmental cues are unreliable and the maintenance of information across many generations might be worth the potential costs.
source: By contrast, transgenerational effects were found to predominantly be favored when parental environmental cues are unreliable and the maintenance of information across many generations might be worth the potential costs (Uller et al., 2015).
evidence: The text explicitly states this claim, citing Uller et al., 2015.

claim: The findings support either a model in which intergenerational and transgenerational effects represent potentially distinct phenomena or a model in which transgenerational effects only persist under certain conditions.
source: Our findings in this study support either a model in which intergenerational and transgenerational effects represent potentially distinct phenomena or a model in which transgenerational effects only persist or occur under certain conditions with the vast majority of the effects of parental stress on offspring gene expression being lost or actively erased after one generation under other conditions.
evidence: The text explicitly states this conclusion based on the F1 and F3 gene expression data.
